data.text:
Booked a Grab from BGC to Makati. What should’ve been an 11-minute wait turned into more than an hour. 

Had I walked, I would’ve arrived earlier and saved PHP 400.

This kind of delay is typical during the Christmas rush, but what happened next wasn’t the usual holiday complaint.

The driver was initially just three minutes away, then I saw his car circling an intersection. A moment later, it went completely off-course and got stuck in heavy traffic. 

I considered cancelling, but something told me to wait.

When I called, the driver explained that a motorcycle had hit his car and sped off. 

A hit-and-run.

When he finally arrived, I saw the damage on his bumper. But the moment I stepped inside, he spoke with calmness and composure, telling me the whole story. 

He had chased down the motorcycle, which tried to hide by turning off its lights near a big tree. With the help of traffic enforcers, he found the rider.

I asked more questions, and his story unfolded.

His name is Tatay Eduardo. One of nine siblings. A Kapampangan. 

He only finished Grade 3 and initially worked as a tricycle driver but eventually put three children through college. 

A nurse, a medtech, and a future policewoman.

He showed me a family photo, beaming with pride.

A decade ago, he met a cosmetics distributor who gave him a shot. He sold his tricycle for PHP 10,000 and became a distributor himself. He sourced products from China, traveled to Baler and Pangasinan, and sold his goods at margins of 10x to 20x. With that income, he paid for his children’s schooling, bought secondhand cars for them, and even purchased a brand-new Toyota Innova.

Then the pandemic hit. Online shopping exploded. His customers discovered the real price of his products, and he was forced to liquidate everything at a loss.

But in the face of a setback, he pivoted.

And that path led him to become a Grab driver today.

He still works extremely hard. He lives in a dorm near SM North EDSA and plies his trade in the morning before restarting late in the afternoon.

He only goes home to Pampanga about twice a month and is determined to finish his kids’ schooling.

“Basta lumaban ng patas, kakayanin.”

In a country where fairness and honesty have become rare, his story gives me a lot of hope.

As long as we continue fighting and pursue an honest living, God will provide.

A damaged bumper, a hit-and-run, and a long wait later, I ended up meeting a man whose life story is a masterclass in grit, reinvention, and the kind of resilience that doesn’t make headlines but keeps this country moving.
